content: Klebsiella is a type of gram-negative bacteria that is naturally present in human stool (feces). While it is part of the normal gut flora, it can cause serious healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) in certain circumstances. These infections include pneumonia, bloodstream infections, wound or surgical site infections, and meningitis. Alarmingly, some strains of Klebsiella are becoming increasingly resistant to antibiotics, including carbapenems, which are often considered the last line of defense against multidrug-resistant bacterial infections. In healthcare settings, individuals who are already ill and undergoing treatment for other conditions are at the highest risk of developing Klebsiella infections. Patients who rely on medical devices such as ventilators (breathing machines) or intravenous (IV) catheters, as well as those on prolonged courses of specific antibiotics, are particularly vulnerable. In contrast, healthy individuals are generally not at risk of contracting Klebsiella infections. Klebsiella primarily spreads through person-to-person contact, often via contaminated hands or surfaces. It can also spread through contact with contaminated water, soil, or medical equipment, such as ventilators or IV catheters. However, it is important to note that Klebsiella does not spread through the air. To prevent the spread of Klebsiella, patients should practice frequent hand hygiene. This includes washing hands before preparing or eating food, before touching the eyes, nose, or mouth, before and after changing wound dressings or bandages, after using the restroom, after blowing the nose, coughing, or sneezing, and after touching hospital surfaces like bed rails, bedside tables, doorknobs, remote controls, or phones. Healthcare workers must adhere to strict infection control protocols to minimize the risk of transmitting Klebsiella to patients. If a Klebsiella infection is suspected, healthcare providers will collect a specimen and send it to a laboratory for testing. This testing not only confirms the presence of the bacteria but also helps determine the most effective treatment options. Treatment typically involves antibiotics, but the growing resistance of some Klebsiella strains to multiple antibiotics poses significant challenges in managing these infections. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) is actively working to address the threat posed by Klebsiella. Their efforts include tracking infections through programs like the Emerging Infections Program and the National Healthcare Safety Network, as well as conducting resistance testing through the Antimicrobial Resistance Laboratory Network. The CDC also provides data on Klebsiella infections through the AR & Patient Safety Portal. Additionally, the CDC collaborates with health departments, federal agencies, healthcare providers, and patients to prevent Klebsiella infections and slow the spread of antibiotic-resistant strains.
